533.title: the departure
533.hook: a king runs after a chariot, and a prince asks the driver to pretend he didn't hear
533.howItsDone: In the text, the departure from Ayodhya moves slowly, and its lasting image is the old king watching the road until even the dust of the wheels is gone.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bark clothes, and Sumitra's verse: think of the forest as Ayodhya. A new week begins, and the chariot moves.

Look back, and you can't leave. Don't look back, and it feels cruel. That's the trouble with driving away from someone standing in a doorway, and it's Rama's trouble now. The charioteer Sumantra has the horses ready. Rama, Sita and Lakshmana climb in, with their weapons, a spade, a basket, and Sita's clothes for fourteen years. As the chariot starts to roll, the whole city starts to run after it.
screen: `LOOK BACK, OR GO ON?` → `THE CHARIOT STARTS TO ROLL.` → `THE CITY RUNS AFTER IT.`

segments.voice: Valmiki fills the streets with noise. People run beside the wheels, calling to Sumantra to slow down so they can see Rama's face a little longer. From the palace comes the old king himself, on foot, with Kausalya, crying: wait, Sumantra, wait. Rama hears his father. He can't bear it, and he can't stop. Go on, he tells the driver quietly. If the king asks later, say you didn't hear. Being told to stop and told to go is pain either way; better to make it short. The chariot pulls away. Dasharatha falls in the dust. His counselors lift him and tell him something old and gentle: when you hope for someone to come back, don't follow them too far. The king watches until even the dust from the wheels is gone. But the people keep following. Old brahmins, too slow to keep up, call after the chariot, and Rama, out of respect, gets down and walks, with Sita and Lakshmana beside him. By evening they reach the Tamasa river, and the whole crowd sleeps on the bank around them. That night Rama lies awake. These people will follow us into the forest, he thinks, and lose their homes. So before dawn he wakes Sumantra. They harness the horses quietly and cross the river, and the driver turns the chariot a little way back toward the city before turning again, so the tracks will confuse anyone following. When the people wake, Rama is gone. They search, can't follow the tracks, and walk home weeping.

segments.voice: Think of someone you had to leave, or who had to leave you, and let the scene come back gently. Breathe in and feel the pull to look back; breathe out and feel the need to go on. Neither is wrong; let the breath hold both, and picture the dust settling.
The departure, part three: the road. The king runs after the chariot, the people follow to the Tamasa, and Rama slips away before dawn to spare them.
Your line: Rama slips away before dawn. A hard goodbye, made kind and short. See you tomorrow.

534.title: Guha the boatman
534.hook: at the edge of the kingdom, on the bank of the Ganga, an old friend is waiting
534.carry: a friend as dear as life
534.howItsDone: Many Hindus honor Guha as a model of devoted friendship; Shringaverapura, near Prayagraj, is visited by pilgrims as the place where Rama met him.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the departure. The road out, the king in the dust, and Rama slipping away from the sleeping crowd at the Tamasa. Today, the Ganga, and a friend.

The chariot crosses river after river, through villages already talking about the prince who's been sent away. At the southern edge of the kingdom of Kosala, Rama turns in the chariot, faces the way they've come, and says goodbye to Ayodhya and its gods. Then they ride on to the Ganga. Near a town called Shringaverapura the river is wide and bright. And on its bank lives someone who has heard Rama is coming.
screen: `RIVER AFTER RIVER.` → `GOODBYE TO AYODHYA.` → `SOMEONE WAITS ON THE GANGA.`

segments.voice: His name is Guha, king of the Nishadas, a people who live by the forest and the river, hunting, fishing and running boats. Valmiki introduces him with one phrase: Rama's friend, as dear to him as his own life. We aren't told how they met; the text simply assumes the friendship is old. Guha comes out with his counselors and his family, carrying food and drink of every kind. Rama sees him from a distance, and before Guha can bow, Rama gets down and embraces him. Then Guha makes an extraordinary offer. This land is yours, as Ayodhya is. Who else gets a guest like you? Stay. Rule here. Rama thanks him warmly and says no. He has vowed to live fourteen years as a forest ascetic, eating only roots and fruit, and he won't break it on his first day. He accepts one thing, and it's not for himself. Please feed the horses. They belong to my father, and he loves them. That night Rama and Sita sleep on the bare ground under a tree, on grass Lakshmana gathers, while Guha and Lakshmana sit up by the fire, keeping watch, bows in hand. In a story full of kings, the first to welcome Rama into exile is a forest king, and Rama answers him with an embrace and the word friend.

segments.voice: Think of a friend who showed up for you when things were bad, without being asked, and picture them coming toward you, as Guha came down to the river. Breathe in the relief of being met; breathe out thanks. If no one comes to mind, picture the friend you'd like to be for someone else.

535.title: Guha the boatman
535.hook: two men keep watch by a fire all night, and in the morning a charioteer is sent home
535.howItsDone: Matted hair, jata, is worn by some Hindu ascetics as a sign of renunciation; in the text Rama and Lakshmana mat their hair with banyan sap on the Ganga's bank.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Guha, king of the Nishadas, Rama's friend as dear as life. Today, the night watch on the riverbank.

The fire is low. Rama and Sita sleep on a bed of grass under a tree, a few feet away. Lakshmana sits up with his bow across his knees, wide awake. Guha comes and sits beside him. Late at night, beside someone outside the family, with the people you love asleep nearby, things get said that daylight keeps in. That's what happens on this riverbank before the night is out.
screen: `A LOW FIRE, A BOW ACROSS THE KNEES.` → `GUHA SITS DOWN BESIDE HIM.`

segments.voice: Guha speaks first, kindly. I've made a comfortable bed for you. Go and sleep. My people and I will keep watch; we know this forest. Nothing will happen to Rama while we're here. Lakshmana says no. How can I sleep, when my brother, who should be lying in a palace, is lying on the ground? Then he says out loud what he's carried all day: the old king, who he thinks won't survive the grief; Kausalya and Sumitra, alone in the palace; the city, emptied of joy. Guha listens, and Valmiki says Guha weeps too as the night goes on. Two men, one grief. In the morning, Rama asks Guha for the milky sap of a banyan tree, and with it he and Lakshmana mat their hair into the coils forest ascetics wear. It's the moment their old life visibly ends. Then Rama turns to Sumantra, the charioteer who has driven them all this way. Go back now. Comfort my father. Tell him we're well. Sumantra begs to stay. Let me come with you. How can I drive an empty chariot into Ayodhya? The people will think I've abandoned you. Rama answers with care: you must go back, so that Kaikeyi believes I've truly left, and stops doubting my father. Sumantra turns the horses for home. Now the only ones left are Rama, Sita, Lakshmana, and a friend with a boat.

segments.voice: Think of a worry you carry for someone else, a parent, a child, a friend, that you haven't said out loud. Say it silently now, in a few plain words, as Lakshmana did to Guha. Then keep watch with it, breathing, the way two people keep watch by a fire.
Jata, the matted coils forest ascetics wear. Guha keeps watch all night beside Lakshmana and weeps with him, and at dawn Rama and Lakshmana take it on before Sumantra is sent home.

536.title: Guha the boatman
536.hook: a boat on the Ganga, Sita's prayer in midstream, and a famous boatman who isn't in Valmiki
536.howItsDone: Hindu pilgrims bathe in the Ganga, offer lamps and flowers to it, and speak to it as Ganga Ma, a mother goddess; in the text, Sita prays to the river in midstream.

segments.voice: Yesterday: jata, matted hair at dawn, after a night when two men shared one grief. Today, across the river.

If you've heard this part of the story at a temple or a family reading, you may remember a boatman who won't let Rama into his boat until he's washed his feet. He's afraid, he says with a grin, that the dust of those feet will turn his wooden boat into a woman, the way it once turned a stone into Ahalya. It's a lovely, funny scene. It comes from a later retelling, Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas. Valmiki's crossing is simpler, with its own quiet center.
screen: `WASH YOUR FEET FIRST.` → `A STORY FROM TULSIDAS.` → `VALMIKI'S CROSSING IS SIMPLER.`

segments.voice: In Valmiki, Guha arranges everything. He has a strong, well-made boat brought down to the bank, with oarsmen ready. Rama thanks him and says goodbye. Sita steps in first, then Lakshmana, then Rama, and the oarsmen push off into the current. In midstream, Sita folds her hands and speaks to the river itself, to Ganga, as a goddess. She asks Ganga to protect Rama through the fourteen years and bring the three of them back safely, and she vows to worship the river with offerings when they return. We won't repeat the prayer here, but its shape matters: the first time the exiles leave dry land, Sita turns the crossing into worship. In Hindu tradition, the Ganga is still this: a goddess and a mother as well as a river, someone you can speak to. The boat reaches the far bank, and they're truly outside the kingdom. Rama sets an order for walking: Lakshmana first, to clear the way, Sita in the middle, Rama last, guarding them both. Guha watches from the far shore until they're gone among the trees. So Valmiki's boatman isn't the comic figure of the later story. He's a king, a friend, a host who kept watch all night and provided the boat. Two retellings, two boatmen. Valmiki's is the one who stays on the bank, watching.

537.title: Bharadvaja
537.hook: smoke rising over the trees means a sage is nearby, at the place where two rivers meet
537.howItsDone: Prayaga, now Prayagraj, is a place of pilgrimage; pilgrims bathe at the Sangam, where the Ganga and Yamuna meet, and the Kumbh Mela is held there.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Ganga, honored as goddess and mother. Sita prayed in midstream, and Guha watched them go. Today, a sage where two rivers meet.

Their first night alone, on the far side of the Ganga, is hard. Valmiki lets Rama's calm slip. He lies awake and worries out loud to Lakshmana: about his father, his mother, what Kaikeyi might do now. He even tells Lakshmana to go back and look after them. Lakshmana refuses. In the morning they walk on, and toward evening they see what a traveler in the forest hopes to see: smoke rising above the trees.
screen: `THE FIRST NIGHT ALONE.` → `RAMA WORRIES OUT LOUD.` → `SMOKE ABOVE THE TREES.`

segments.voice: Rama knows what the smoke means. That's the smoke of a sacred fire, he tells Lakshmana. A sage must live there. We must be near Prayaga, where the Ganga and the Yamuna meet; you can hear the two rivers crashing together. They follow the smoke to the hermitage of Bharadvaja, a great sage sitting by his fire among his students. Rama introduces the three of them and explains they've been sent to the forest by his father's command. Bharadvaja, it turns out, already knows. I've been expecting you, he says. I heard you'd been sent away for no fault of your own. He welcomes them as honored guests, with water for their feet, a cow, and food of the forest, fruit and roots. Then an offer. Stay here, at the meeting of the rivers. It's holy, and beautiful. You can live here for the fourteen years. Rama answers thoughtfully. It's too close to home. The people of the cities will hear I'm here and keep coming to see Sita and me. Find us somewhere more secluded. That's worth a pause. Rama turns down comfort and holiness, not because they're bad, but because he wants the exile to be a real exile, and the people back home to let him go. Bharadvaja understands at once, and says he knows just the place. Tonight, the three exiles sleep in a sage's hermitage, by the meeting of two rivers.
screen: `THE SMOKE OF A SACRED FIRE.` · `PRAYAGA: WHERE TWO RIVERS MEET.` · `I'VE BEEN EXPECTING YOU.` · `TOO CLOSE TO HOME.` · then, large: `A SAGE WHO UNDERSTANDS AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Rama knew where he was by a sound and a sign: water meeting water, smoke above the trees. Let the breath be easy, and notice what you can hear: the farthest sound first, then a nearer one, then the nearest, your own breathing. Rest with whatever reaches you.

538.title: Bharadvaja
538.hook: a sage gives directions the old way: a raft, a dark banyan tree, and a mountain you can see from far off
538.howItsDone: In the text, Sita honors the Yamuna as she honored the Ganga; in Hindu tradition the Yamuna is worshiped as a goddess, and Prayagraj and Chitrakoot are both pilgrim places today.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bharadvaja, the sage where the rivers meet, who had been expecting them. Today, his directions.

Before maps on phones, directions were stories. Go past the old mill, turn at the big oak, and when you see the water tower, you're nearly there. Bharadvaja gives Rama directions like that the next morning: a river to cross, a tree to look for, a grove to walk through, and then a mountain. He's sending them to the place where they'll make their first home in exile, and he describes it with love.
screen: `DIRECTIONS WERE STORIES.` → `A RIVER, A TREE, A GROVE.` → `THEN A MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: There's a mountain, Bharadvaja says, about ten kroshas from here, called Chitrakuta. Sages live there. Peacocks call on its slopes, monkeys and langurs play in the trees, and there's fruit and honey everywhere: a good place for someone who wants to live simply and well. Then the route. Follow the Yamuna until you find a crossing. Build a raft, and cross. On the other side you'll find a great banyan with dark leaves, called Shyama, the dark one. Many beings live in it, and people pray there. Walk on past it to a grove, and the road to the mountain. Bharadvaja blesses them, and the three set off. At the river, Rama and Lakshmana gather bamboo and dry wood, tie it together with creepers, and make a raft, and Lakshmana builds Sita a little seat of branches and leaves. In the middle of the Yamuna, as on the Ganga, Sita folds her hands and speaks to the river, asking for her husband's safe return and vowing offerings when they come home. On the far bank they find the dark banyan, exactly where the sage said it would be. Sita bows to it and prays again, for Rama, for Lakshmana, for the day they'll see their mothers. Every crossing is marked with a prayer; every landmark is something holy. Bharadvaja hasn't just given them directions. He's given them a pilgrimage.

539.howItsDone: Many Hindu families hold a griha pravesha, a house-entering ceremony, before moving into a new home; in the text, Rama blesses the leaf hut at Chitrakuta before the three exiles enter it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bharadvaja, part two. A raft across the Yamuna, the dark banyan, and a mountain of peacocks and honey. Today they arrive.

The forest is in flower. Rama walks with Sita, and for the first time since Ayodhya, he sounds almost happy. Look, he tells her: the flame-of-the-forest trees are in bloom, so red they look on fire. Honeycombs hang from the branches, big as buckets. Listen to the birds. Then the trees open, and there it is: a mountain with many peaks, streams running down its sides. Chitrakuta.
screen: `THE FOREST IN FLOWER.` → `TREES THAT LOOK ON FIRE.` → `THERE IT IS: CHITRAKUTA.`

segments.voice: Chitrakuta, or Chitrakoot as many say it today, means something like the bright peak, or the many-colored peak. It lives up to its name. Rama decides at once: we'll live here. But first, a visit. On the mountain, the text says, is the hermitage of a sage, and the three exiles bow to him. The sage is Valmiki. Enjoy that for a second: the poet telling this whole story appears inside it, welcoming the hero he's writing about. The Ramayana does this from its first pages. Valmiki hears Rama's story from Narada, and later, Sita's sons will grow up in his hermitage. Here he simply greets them, and they sit with him a while. Then the work. Lakshmana gathers wood and leaves and builds a hut, a parnashala, a house of leaves, strong against wind and rain, with a door and a thatched roof. Before they move in, Rama performs a rite to bless the house, as a family would for a new home, with offerings to the gods of the dwelling. Then the three of them step inside. Look how far this week has carried them: a chariot leaving a weeping city, a night by the Tamasa, a friend on the Ganga, a night watch, a crossing with a prayer in midstream, a sage where the rivers meet, a raft and a dark banyan. And now a home of leaves on a bright mountain, with a poet next door.
